title: Let Him Kiss Me: The Song Begins with Longing
summary: After a title naming the Song of Songs, a woman speaks her longing for her beloved and asks him to take her away. She tells the daughters of Jerusalem that she is dark from working in the sun, yet lovely, and asks where her beloved shepherds his flock. The two lovers then exchange words of praise, comparing each other to fragrant spices, doves, and a house built of cedar.
story: The Bible's wisdom books have moved from Proverbs, with its practical counsel for life under God, to Ecclesiastes, with its honest search for what lasts in a fleeting world. The Song of Songs takes a different path. It sings of love between a woman and a man, and it begins not with an explanation but in the middle of desire. There is no narrator setting the scene, no introduction of characters by name, only a woman's voice saying what she wants. This opening chapter establishes the book's main speakers (the woman, the man, and a group the woman addresses as the daughters of Jerusalem), its two worlds of royal court and countryside, and its language of fragrance, vineyards, and flocks. What follows in the rest of the Song grows from these first images.
historical: The title connects the Song with Solomon, who reigned over Israel in the tenth century BC and was remembered for his wisdom, wealth, and many songs (1 Kings 4:32). Whether he wrote the Song, or whether it was written about him or dedicated to him, is debated, as the introduction explains. The chapter mentions Pharaoh's chariots (verse 9), and Solomon's reign had close ties to Egypt: he married a daughter of Pharaoh and imported horses and chariots from Egypt (1 Kings 3:1; 10:28-29). Kedar (verse 5) was a tribe of the north Arabian desert, known from the prophets (Isaiah 21:16-17; Jeremiah 49:28). En-gedi (verse 14) is a real oasis on the western shore of the Dead Sea, fed by springs in the desert cliffs, which in the ancient world was famous for its vegetation.
cultural:
The woman's explanation that she is dark because the sun has gazed on her (verse 6) reflects the difference between those who worked outdoors and those who did not. In the ancient Near East, as in many societies, pale skin was associated with wealth and leisure, while sun-darkened skin marked a laborer. Her brothers have made her work in the vineyards, and she has had no time to tend her own vineyard, which most readers take as a picture of her own person or beauty. Kedar's tents were woven from black goat hair, and the curtains of Solomon were presumably fine and costly, so she compares herself to both: dark, yet beautiful.

The man is pictured as both a king (verses 4 and 12) and a shepherd (verse 7). Many interpreters think these are not two different men but two ways of seeing the same beloved; in ancient love poetry, as in Egyptian love songs, lovers often picture each other in royal or pastoral roles. A veiled woman wandering among shepherds (verse 7) might be mistaken for a woman of loose reputation, which is why she wants to know exactly where to find him. The perfumes of the chapter (nard, myrrh, and henna) were luxury goods, and a sachet of myrrh worn around the neck was a way of carrying fragrance through the day.
literary: The chapter is a series of short speeches, and much of the interpretive work is deciding who is speaking. Hebrew marks the gender of many words, so readers can often tell whether the woman or the man is being addressed, though translations that add speaker headings are making educated judgments. The woman speaks most of the chapter (verses 2 to 7, 12 to 14, and 16 to 17); the man answers in verses 8 to 11 and 15; the we of verses 4 and 11 may be the daughters of Jerusalem or the man and his companions. The poetry moves quickly between third person and second person (let him kiss me, your love is better than wine), a feature common in ancient love poetry that conveys longing for someone both present and absent. The chapter ends with the lovers praising each other in matching words (how beautiful you are, how handsome you are), a pattern of mutual praise that recurs through the book.

outline.t: The woman longs for her beloved's love
Where do you pasture your flock?
He praises her beauty and adornment
Myrrh and henna: her delight in him
Mutual praise, and a house of cedar

doctrines.note: The chapter delights in the body, fragrance, beauty, and desire without embarrassment. This fits the Bible's first chapters, where God makes humanity male and female and calls his creation very good. Love and attraction between a man and a woman belong to that goodness.

The woman's longing is directed to one beloved, whom she seeks by name and place. The Song pictures love as personal and exclusive, the kind of bond Scripture elsewhere calls marriage, and it gives the woman a full voice in it.

words.note: Dod, love, often in the plural (loves or caresses) and meaning expressions of love. In verse 2 the woman says your love is more delightful than wine, and the word appears again in verse 4. The same root gives the word for beloved (dodi, my beloved), which becomes the woman's name for the man throughout the book.

Dod, beloved. In verses 13 and 14 the woman calls the man my beloved, a title she uses more than two dozen times in the Song. It is the characteristic word of her voice. Allegorical readers heard in it the name of God or Christ as the beloved of his people; natural readers hear a woman's affectionate name for the man she loves.

Rayah, my darling, a feminine word related to the word for friend or companion. It is the man's characteristic name for the woman, used first in verse 9 and repeated throughout the Song. The word suggests companionship as well as romance: she is his beloved and his friend.

Shachor, black or dark. In verse 5 the woman says she is dark, yet lovely, and in verse 6 she explains that the sun has darkened her. The word here refers to sun-darkened skin from outdoor labor, not to ethnicity. Many later readers have found in the verse a word of dignity for anyone told that their appearance disqualifies them from beauty, and the text itself affirms her loveliness.

christ: The New Testament does not quote this chapter, and any connection to Christ comes through the wider biblical theme of God's love for his people pictured as the love of a bridegroom. Jewish readers heard in the woman's longing the voice of Israel longing for God, and in the kisses of his mouth the words God spoke to his people. Christian readers from Origen in the third century to Bernard of Clairvaux, whose early sermons on the Song dwell on the kiss of verse 2, heard the church or the individual believer longing for Christ. These readings belong to a long tradition but are readings, not claims made by the text itself. Readers who take the Song first as human love poetry see a link of a different kind: the delight of lovers in each other, rightly ordered, reflects the delight God takes in his people, which the prophets express as a bridegroom's joy over his bride (Isaiah 62:5), and which the New Testament ties to Christ, the bridegroom (Mark 2:19-20).

hard.q: Why is a book about romantic and physical love in the Bible at all?
hard.a: The question is old. Early Jewish and Christian readers who valued the Song defended its place by reading it as an allegory of God's love, and according to the Mishnah Rabbi Akiva, in the early second century AD, insisted that it was the holiest of the Writings. Many modern readers give a different answer: the Song belongs in Scripture because love between a man and a woman is part of the good world God made, and people need wisdom for it as much as for money, speech, or work. The Bible does not treat the body as shameful; Genesis 2 ends with the man and woman naked and unashamed. The Song affirms that goodness while also setting love within faithfulness, exclusivity, and patience. Many readers today hold both answers: the Song is in the Bible because human love is good, and because human love at its best points to the love of God for his people.

questions: The Song opens with a woman speaking frankly about her desire. How does it change your picture of the Bible to find this voice in it?
The woman is self-conscious about her appearance but also says she is lovely. How do you think about your own body in light of the Bible's claim that God made it good?
The lovers praise each other in matching words. What would it look like to speak words of appreciation to someone you love this week?
